<reason>Both sides were competent and the clash was genuinely tight, but CON narrowed the debate to the decisive question—what actually determines Iran's distance to a bomb—and won it. CON established that the surviving, relocated HEU plus a small warehouse cascade is the real timeline, that the industrial "spine" PRO destroyed was the already-completed part, and that the strikes removed the one mechanism (sealed feedstock under IAEA watch) that made any future "veto" locatable and executable. PRO's best attack—the alleged contradiction between "warehouse sprint" and "inspectors keep it honest"—was cleanly reconciled in CON's A2 (cameras guarded the material, so diversion was the alarm that enabled a strike). CON also won the Osirak exchange with accurate history (covert program found near-complete in 1991, ended by inspections not the raid) and the diplomacy exchange (60% enrichment post-dates the JCPOA exit; Iran honored caps for three years). PRO's strongest surviving material—nuclear immunity/proliferation cascade, and the "consent-dependent subscription" framing—was memorable but never fully re-engaged with CON's feedstock-under-seal point, and PRO's inability to offer any magnitude for the setback left the risk/benefit comparison the motion demands underdetermined. CON's two clipped turns are a real execution cost, but the lost material was marginal and does not offset the substantive edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's A2 answering PRO's Q2/[B4.5] "tears itself in half" charge: conceding inspectors were a "notification service" but showing notification of a broken seal on watched feedstock is precisely what converts a weeks-long sprint into a known-location strike window—so the strikes "did Iran's diversion for it" and kept none of the alarm. This neutralized PRO's sharpest attack and flipped it into support for CON's rubble-for-eyes ledger.</best_rebuttal>
